title: How Long Does a Penetration Test Take in 2026?
summary: A traditional pentest takes 2 to 6 weeks from contract to report. CodeAnt AI delivers the report in 48 hours. See each phase and how to plan.

A traditional penetration test takes about two to six weeks from signed contract to final report.[Schellman](https://www.schellman.com/video/penetration-testing/how-long-does-a-penetration-test-take) puts a small external test at about two weeks and an average scope at four to five weeks, and[Triaxiom Security](https://www.triaxiomsecurity.com/?p=1897) describes a typical project as four to six weeks, of which active testing is one to two. Most of that time is scheduling and report writing, not testing.[CodeAnt AI](https://codeant.ai/pentesting) delivers a full pentest report within 48 hours, with every critical finding confirmed by a security researcher, so the time left on your calendar is the time your team needs to fix and retest. It fits security and engineering leads who owe an auditor, an enterprise customer or an investor a pentest report by a fixed date.


CodeAnt AI has run 12,000 pentests and is trusted by more than 1,000 companies, including Fortune 500 companies like NRG, cybersecurity leaders like Commvault, and fast-growing companies like 11x and Sanas.


Buyers rarely ask how many hours of testing they are buying. They ask whether the report will be ready before the audit, the customer review or the funding round closes. This guide answers that: how long each phase takes, what published turnarounds from six providers actually measure, and how to plan backward from your deadline.


## How Long Does Each Phase of a Penetration Test take?


NIST's guide to security testing ([SP 800-115](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-115.pdf) ) splits a penetration test into four phases: planning, discovery, attack and reporting, with reporting running alongside the other three. NIST also calls penetration testing labor-intensive work that requires great expertise, which is why a traditional engagement is booked in weeks. ## What Makes a Penetration Test Take Longer?


Testing hours are rarely what pushes a pentest past a deadline. These are:


-


**Access that is not ready.** A black box test needs only your domain, because the tester discovers your exposed surface the way an attacker would. A grey box test needs working test accounts, ideally at the lowest privilege level, and a way past MFA or SSO. A white box test needs access to your code repository or cloud account. A login step the tester cannot pass delays the start.


-


**Scope.** More applications, APIs, networks and user roles mean more to test. Schellman notes that its longest engagements combine several services, such as web apps, mobile apps and internal and external networks.


-


**Production windows.** If your systems scale down at weekends or you want testing outside business hours, agree the window before the start date.


-


**Authorization.** Every system in scope needs written permission, including assets hosted by a third party. Our[pentest authorization letter template](https://codeant.ai/blogs/pentest-authorization-letter-template) covers what to include.


-


**Fixes.** Remediation is your team's time, and a release freeze or a holiday week can double it.


-


**The vendor's queue.** Traditional firms schedule testers weeks ahead. Triaxiom's planning phase alone is two to three weeks.


Not sure which test type you need? See[black box vs grey box vs white box penetration testing](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/black-box-vs-white-box-vs-gray-box-penetration-testing) .


## How Do You Fit a Pentest Before a SOC 2 Audit or Customer Deadline?


Plan backward from the date someone else needs your report:


1.


**Find the date.** Ask your auditor, customer or investor when they need the report, which version they want (many ask only for the executive summary), and, for an audit, which period the test must fall in.


2.


**Subtract your fix time.** Ask your engineers how long they need to fix high and critical findings, then add a buffer for release freezes and holidays.


3.


**Subtract test and report time.** That is 48 hours at CodeAnt AI, or two to six weeks for a traditional engagement once scheduling and report writing are included.


4.


**Subtract setup.** Agree the scope, sign the authorization, and have test accounts and login access ready on the first day.


Worked example: your auditor needs the final report on the 1st of the month, and your engineers need ten working days to fix what a test finds. With a 48-hour AI-led pentest, start about three weeks before the deadline: two days for the test and report, two weeks of fixes, and a few days of buffer for the retest and setup. With a traditional engagement of four to six weeks plus the same two weeks of fixes, you would need to sign roughly two months ahead.


If you test before every audit anyway, a continuous program removes most of this planning. See[continuous vs annual pentesting](https://codeant.ai/blogs/continuous-vs-annual-pentesting) and how[compliance automation and penetration testing fit together for SOC 2](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/compliance-automation-vs-penetration-testing-soc-2) .


## Does a Faster Pentest Mean a Shallower One?


Not if the speed comes from removing waiting rather than removing testing. In a traditional engagement, much of the calendar is the queue before testers start and the week of report writing after they finish. In an AI-led pentest, agents work the attack surface continuously, chain issues into attack paths and prove what an attacker could actually reach, and security researchers confirm the critical findings before they reach you.


What speed does not change:


-


**Your fix time.** A faster report gets findings to your engineers sooner; it does not fix them.


-


**Very large or unusual scopes.** Red team exercises and multi-part engagements still run for weeks with any provider.


-


**What your reviewer accepts.** Ask your auditor or customer which report they need before you buy, and check the provider's own terms. Cobalt states its Autonomous Pentest does not produce compliance attestation reports; Synack's compliance-ready report starts with its SynackST tier. CodeAnt AI's report is ready for SOC 2 and ISO 27001.


For what auditors look for in a pentest, see our guide to[SOC 2 penetration testing requirements](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/soc-2-penetration-testing-requirements) .
